catalog_quote: [p.33, sec. 4.2 PWB phonological word] Most WB languages are sesquisyllabic-a word may consist of one or one and a half syllables. In the latter case a stressed mainsyllable is preceded by a minorsyllable, a structurally impoverished unit that is constructed from a restricted set of segments. The minorsyllable typically consists of an oral stop or fricative of unmarked phonation type, an epenthetic ([a] or schwa-like) vowel, and may be closed by a nasal or rhotic. ... [p.34] On the Plateau itself there is a tendency to shift sequisyllabic words into monosyllables, and the extreme example is Nyaheun, in which almost all words are now CV(F) or CRV(F). ... [p.22, sec. 3.5 Nyaheun] Phonologically Nyaheun is quite aberrant. The phonological word is both compact and complex, yet the language is without tones or registers. All three quoted passages are present verbatim at the stated locators (ellipses in the report mark genuine omissions only): PDF p.43 = book p.33, sec. 4.2 'PWB phonological word': 'Most WB languages are sesquisyllabic-a word may consist of one or one and a half syllables. In the latter case a stressed mainsyllable is preceded by a minorsyllable, a structurally impoverished unit..'; PDF p.44 = p.34: 'On the Plateau itself there is a tendency to shift sequisyllabic words into monosyllables, and the extreme example is Nyaheun, in which almost all words are now CV(F)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: West Bahnaric words are monosyllables or iambic sesquisyllables with stress on the (final) main syllable; Nyaheun has carried monosyllabization furthest, so native words are single stressed C(R)V(F) syllables (no tone, no register); the few residual non-monosyllables (C+glottal-stop onsets, e.g. t?ak 'brain') have only a ~40 ms epenthetic vowel before the main syllable, i.e. prominence is on the final/main syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: p.24: 'The few exceptions to the monosyllabic pattern in native vocabulary involve words with consonant + ? onsets.. pronounced with a short (~40ms) epenthetic vowel separating the initial cluster'; recent Jru' loans with final /r/ vocalise to an extra open syllable ([ara]). Watson 1969 p.130 notes variable prominence between onglide and vowel inside diphthongal nuclei.
new_statements.domain_note: The explicit 'stressed mainsyllable' clause is a family-level (West Bahnaric) statement in the same book; the Nyaheun-specific profile states monosyllabic C(R)V(F) word structure without tones/registers rather than using the word 'stress'. Word-level (lexical citation forms from Jacq's draft dictionary); nothing on phrasal prominence or compounds.
new_statements.identity_note: Sidwell & Jacq 2003 describe Nyaheun (autonym given as [hə̃ən]-like form; also Nhaheun, Yaheun, Nyahon) of the western Boloven Plateau (Ban Thongvay / Houeikong / Senamnoy area), principal consultant Dot (Done) Launmeuang, who was also Davis's 1960s informant; same variety as Glottolog nyah1249 / ISO nev. No dialect split is reported.

sources.note: Sec. 4.2 p.33: in WB sesquisyllables 'a stressed mainsyllable is preceded by a minorsyllable'; p.34: Nyaheun is the extreme monosyllabizer, 'almost all words are now CV(F) or CRV(F)'. Nyaheun profile sec. 3.5 pp.22-24: 'without tones or registers', whole lexicon C(R)V(F) monosyllables, the handful of exceptions (C+glottal-stop onsets) have a ~40 ms epenthetic vowel. No Nyaheun-specific sentence using the word 'stress'.
